t:
Nothing in title XIX of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.) shall be construed as prohibiting separate payment under the State plan under such title (or under a waiver of the plan) for the provision of a mental health service or primary care service under such plan, with respect to an individual, because such service is—
    (1) a primary care service furnished to the individual by a provider at a facility on the same day a mental health service is furnished to such individual by such provider (or another provider) at the facility; or 
    (2) a mental health service furnished to the individual by a provider at a facility on the same day a primary care service is furnished to such individual by such provider (or another provider) at the facility.

fable.w: This is a rule of construction clarifying that Medicaid does not bar separate payment for same-day mental health and primary care services. The tempting reading is that the reference to a "State plan" implies federal-state coordination, but the section sets up no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue. No outside party is brought into any federal decision.
fable.s: Nothing in title XIX of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.) shall be construed as prohibiting separate payment under the State plan under such title

It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or decision-making process involving parties outside the federal government. The text is purely regulatory regarding reimbursement mechanisms.

opus.w: This is a rule of construction about Medicaid payment. It allows separate payment for a primary care service and a mental health service delivered on the same day. Nothing in it requires or allows any outside party to be consulted, heard, or given a way to challenge a federal decision. Mentioning a 'State plan' or 'waiver' does not mean a state is involved in a federal decision; it only names the payment framework.
opus.s: Nothing in title XIX of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.) shall be construed as prohibiting separate payment under the State plan under such title (or under a waiver of the plan)
opus.b:
1. **Thinking it through.** The tempting reading is that "the State plan under such title (or under a waiver of the plan)" means states are working with the federal government on Medicaid decisions. That doesn't hold up. The section is only a rule of construction: it says Medicaid can't be read to bar separate payment for a primary care service and a mental health service given on the same day. It sets up no consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body, rulemaking authority or right to sue. A state plan or waiver is closer to an application than to taking part in a federal decision.

2. **Label.**

qwen_chat.w: This section clarifies payment rules for healthcare services under a state plan. It does not require the federal government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties (such as states, tribes, or the public) before making a decision. It merely defines when separate payments are permitted, which is a substantive rule rather than a participatory process.

qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the section allows for separate payments for services provided to individuals, it involves interaction with the public. However, this is merely a clarification of payment rules for healthcare providers under a state plan, not a requirement for the federal government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties before making a decision. The section does not establish a process for public comment, advisory boards, or consultation with states/tribes regarding federal policy decisions; it simply defines eligibility for payment.
